healthTips.title: Drink Enough Water Every Day
healthTips.shortDescription: Staying hydrated supports energy, digestion and concentration. Learn simple ways to drink more water.
healthTips.content:
Water makes up a large part of the human body and plays a role in almost every function, from digestion to temperature control.

How much do you need? A common guideline is around 8 glasses (about 2 litres) a day, but your needs depend on your body size, activity level and the weather.

Simple ways to drink more:
• Keep a water bottle on your desk or bag.
• Drink a glass after waking up and before each meal.
• Add a slice of lemon, cucumber or mint for flavor.
• Drink extra water in hot weather and during exercise.

Dark yellow urine is a sign that you may need more water. If you have a medical condition that affects fluids, follow your doctor's advice.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Eat a Balanced Plate at Every Meal
healthTips.shortDescription: A simple plate model helps you build meals with vegetables, protein and whole grains.
healthTips.content:
You do not need a complicated diet plan to eat well. A simple method is to divide your plate into sections:

• Half the plate: colorful vegetables and fruit.
• One quarter: protein such as fish, chicken, eggs, pulses or meat.
• One quarter: whole grains such as brown rice, whole wheat roti or oats.

Tips:
• Choose water instead of sugary drinks.
• Limit fried food and salty snacks.
• Eat seasonal local fruits and vegetables — they are fresh and affordable.

Small, consistent changes make a bigger difference than a perfect one-day diet.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Child Immunization: What Parents Should Know
healthTips.shortDescription: Vaccines protect children from serious diseases. Know the schedule and where to get them.
healthTips.content:
Immunization is one of the safest and most effective ways to protect your child from serious diseases such as measles, polio and diphtheria.

Key points:
• Follow the national immunization schedule provided at your local health center.
• Keep your child's vaccination card safe and bring it to every visit.
• Common mild side effects like a slight fever or soreness are normal and usually pass quickly.
• If your child misses a dose, talk to a health worker about the best time to catch up.

Vaccines are free at government health facilities. If you are unsure about anything, ask your health worker.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Iron and Folic Acid in Pregnancy
healthTips.shortDescription: Iron and folic acid support both mother and baby. Simple facts for expecting mothers.
healthTips.content:
During pregnancy the body needs more iron and folic acid to support the growing baby and prevent anemia.

Why it matters:
• Folic acid in early pregnancy helps the baby's brain and spine develop.
• Iron prevents anemia, which causes tiredness and weakness.

What to do:
• Take the iron and folic acid tablets given at your antenatal checkup as instructed.
• Eat iron-rich foods: dark leafy vegetables, lentils, eggs and red meat.
• Vitamin C (lemon, orange, tomato) helps the body absorb iron.

Always discuss supplements with your doctor — do not take extra doses on your own.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Five Steps to Better Sleep
healthTips.shortDescription: Poor sleep affects mood, memory and health. These five habits can help you rest better.
healthTips.content:
Adults generally need 7-9 hours of sleep per night. Good sleep improves memory, mood and immunity.

Five simple habits:
1. Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends.
2. Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and cool.
3. Avoid screens (phone, TV) for 30-60 minutes before bed.
4. Avoid large meals, tea or coffee in the late evening.
5. Wind down with a book, light stretching or deep breathing.

If you regularly struggle to sleep despite these habits, speak with a healthcare professional.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Men's Health: Regular Checkups Matter
healthTips.shortDescription: A quick checkup can catch problems early. Which tests should men discuss with a doctor?
healthTips.content:
Many men skip health checkups until something feels wrong. Regular checkups can catch conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes early, when they are easier to manage.

Discuss these with your doctor:
• Blood pressure measurement.
• Blood sugar and cholesterol tests.
• Height, weight and BMI.
• Any persistent symptoms like chest pain, fatigue or changes in urination.

If you have a family history of heart disease or diabetes, mention it to your doctor — you may need earlier or more frequent screening.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Start Moving: 30 Minutes a Day
healthTips.shortDescription: You don't need a gym. Walking and simple home exercises are enough to start.
healthTips.content:
Physical activity reduces the risk of heart disease, diabetes and depression. The goal for most adults is about 30 minutes of moderate activity on most days.

Easy ways to start:
• Walk briskly for 20-30 minutes after a meal.
• Take the stairs instead of the lift.
• Do simple stretching or bodyweight exercises at home.
• Involve family or friends — it is easier to stay motivated together.

Start slowly and build up gradually. If you have a health condition, check with your doctor before starting a new exercise routine.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Wash Your Hands, Protect Your Family
healthTips.shortDescription: Handwashing is the simplest way to stop infections from spreading. When and how to wash.
healthTips.content:
Regular handwashing with soap and water is one of the most effective ways to prevent diarrhea, respiratory infections and other diseases.

Wash your hands:
• Before eating or preparing food.
• After using the toilet.
• After coughing, sneezing or touching public surfaces.
• After coming home from outside.

How to wash properly: wet hands, apply soap, rub all surfaces for at least 20 seconds (sing 'Happy Birthday' twice), rinse and dry with a clean towel.

If soap and water are not available, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Limit Salt and Sugar for a Healthier Heart
healthTips.shortDescription: Too much salt and sugar is linked to high blood pressure and diabetes. Easy swaps to try.
healthTips.content:
Most people consume more salt and sugar than they need, which increases the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease and diabetes.

Easy swaps:
• Use less salt while cooking and taste food before adding more.
• Choose fresh food over packaged snacks, which often hide salt and sugar.
• Drink water, lemon water or unsweetened tea instead of sugary soft drinks.
• Read the label: look at how much sugar and sodium the product contains.

Your taste buds adjust within a few weeks — food starts to taste right with less salt and sugar.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Know Your Blood Pressure Numbers
healthTips.shortDescription: High blood pressure often has no symptoms. Understand the numbers and when to act.
healthTips.content:
Blood pressure is written as two numbers, for example 120/80. The first number (systolic) measures pressure when the heart beats; the second (diastolic) measures pressure between beats.

General ranges (for adults):
• Normal: below 120/80.
• Elevated: 120-129 / below 80.
• High: 130 or higher / 80 or higher.

High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, which is why regular measurement matters. If your reading is high, check it again and see a doctor. Lifestyle changes — less salt, more activity, healthy weight, quitting tobacco — can make a big difference.

This information is not medical advice. Always discuss your readings with a healthcare professional.
healthTips.author: Doctor Care BD Editorial

healthTips.title: Beat the Heat: Staying Safe in Hot Weather
healthTips.shortDescription: High temperatures can be dangerous. Simple habits keep you cool and hydrated.
healthTips.content:
Hot weather can cause dehydration, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, especially for children, the elderly and people with chronic illness.

Stay safe in the heat:
• Drink water regularly even if you do not feel thirsty.
• Avoid going outside during the hottest part of the day (11 AM - 3 PM).
• Wear light, loose clothing and a hat when outdoors.
• Keep cool with fans, shade and cool showers.
• Never leave children or elderly people in a parked car.

Seek urgent help if someone shows signs of heat stroke: very high body temperature, confusion, rapid pulse or loss of consciousness.
